paper_title: Open-HumanWAM: An Open Recipe for Scaling Human and Robot Experience for Embodied Foundation Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Egocentric human video offers a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, yet translating raw data scale into generalizable robot policies demands rigorous data curation and training recipes. We introduce Open-HumanWAM, the first fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining to 50,000 hours, anchored by Open-HumanWAM-50K---a curated egocentric video corpus densely annotated with hand motion and natural language. Leveraging this corpus, we systematically investigate pure human pretraining via closed-loop simulation evaluations and uncover an empirical log-linear scaling law linking pretraining data hours to downstream robot success rates. Grounded in these findings, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, a world--action model pretrained exclusively on 50k hours of egocentric human video. Upon robot post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, alongside a 14.17% mean success rate and a 19.00 mean progress score on RoboDojo. To push the capability frontier further, we explore joint human--robot pretraining with HumanWAM-Goal, a visual-goal-conditioned world--action model. Hybrid data scaling unlocks broad zero-shot generalization across both simulation and physical benchmarks, propelling post-trained RoboTwin 2.0 performance to new state-of-the-art levels: 92.70% on Clean2Clean and a substantial leap to 84.60% on Clean2Random. On physical robots, HumanWAM-Goal further exhibits emergent embodied in-context learning, dynamically adapting its manipulation behavior to unseen visual goals without parameter updates. To support reproducible scaling research in embodied AI, we open-source the Open-HumanWAM-50K corpus, data curation and pretraining pipelines, alongside the pretrained and post-trained HumanWAM checkpoints, inference code, and simulation evaluation suites.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Figure 1 Overview of Open-HumanWAM. Using curated 50,000-hour egocentric corpus, we show that scaling human data improves robot generalization after post-training, with greater task and scene diversity yielding steeper scaling curves. We then extend this pretraining approach to combine human and robot data, finding that hybrid scaling improves zero-shot success in simulation and across 20 real-world tasks. Learning from human manipulation offers scalable path toward general-purpose robot intelligence [22, 33, 73]. Robot foundation models require diverse manipulation experience to acquire skills that transfer across tasks and environments, but collecting this experience through teleoperation is costly [22, 23]. Egocentric videos paired with hand-motion and language annotations offer rich record of human interactions with objects across diverse scenes and tasks [20, 43]. However, developing effective egocentric pretraining recipes that consistently improve downstream robot performance as data scale remains under investigation. Previous work has demonstrated the value of human experience for robot learning. EgoScale [73] shows that large-scale human motion pretraining improves dexterous robot manipulation, while Being-H0.8 [4] extends egocentric pretraining to joint visual and tactile world modeling. HumanScale [33] further shows that, after robot post-training, validation action loss on held-out real-robot trajectories decreases log-linearly with egocentric pretraining hours. Dyna-2 [14] extends egocentric pretraining to one million hours and reports scaling law in zero-shot robot action prediction, with corresponding improvements in robot task performance after post-training. These studies establish the empirical value of egocentric scaling, motivating further analysis of data diversity and the robot supervision required for downstream adaptation. We present Open-HumanWAM, fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining for robot learning. Within unified worldaction model framework, we explore pretraining exclusively on 100 to 50,000 hours of human egocentric data, using common robot post-training protocol and closed-loop simulation for controlled and reproducible comparisons of downstream robot task success. With curated data and unified action representation, we observe an empirical log-linear scaling law relating pretraining hours to out-of-distribution success rates across two different attention configurations. Beyond duration, data diversity is key scaling dimension, as expanding task and scene coverage alongside duration produces steeper scaling curves than increasing duration at fixed coverage. Larger-scale egocentric pretraining also improves the sample efficiency of robot adaptation, yielding higher success rates at matched demonstration budgets. Following this recipe, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, vanilla worldaction model pretrained exclusively on 50,000 hours of egocentric human data. After robot post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla achieves 92.08% success on RoboTwin 2.0 [8] Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, together with mean success rate of 14.17% and mean progress score of 19.00 on RoboDojo [9]. The improvements extend to physical robots across multi-step, deformable-object, and long-horizon manipulation tasks. Under changes in tablecloth and lighting, mean success across four tasks increases from 2.5% without egocentric pretraining to 67.5% with HumanWAM-Vanilla, demonstrating stronger generalization. To further push the model capability boundary, we extend our exploration to joint human-robot pretraining and propose HumanWAM-Goal, worldaction model with visual-goal conditioning. Human data provide broad manipulation experience, while robot data ground this experience in embodiment-specific perception and control [25, 73]. Visual goals specify desired object configurations and spatial relationships, providing task context for zero-shot execution. With the specially designed unified action representation, HumanWAM-Goal architecture, and the hybrid training recipe, the co-trained model supports out-of-the-box execution without parameter updates during deployment. We evaluate data scaling by expanding the robot corpus and the human data. The performance scaling trend persists in this hybrid data setting. On physical robots, adding 45.9k hours of human data to fixed 14.6k-hour robot corpus increases mean zero-shot success across 20 tasks from 20.0% to 30.5%. On RoboTwin 2.0, HumanWAM-Goal achieves 13.94% mean zero-shot success rate. After post-training, it reaches 92.70% on Clean2Clean and 84.60% on Clean2Random, yielding state-of-the-art average success rate of 88.65% on RoboTwin 2.0. HumanWAM-Goal exhibits an emergent capacity for embodied in-context learning through visual goals. In real-robot experiments, the same policy adapts its execution to different desired outcomes specified by goal images without parameter updates. This capability is already present after joint pretraining and is retained when the model is post-trained for more complex, multi-step manipulation. Post-trained policies also follow goals depicted in egocentric human images, indicating that task-relevant spatial relationships can guide robot behavior across differences in embodiment and visual appearance. To support reproducible scaling research in embodied AI, we open-source the Open-HumanWAM-50K corpus, data curation and pretraining pipelines, alongside the pretrained and post-trained HumanWAM checkpoints, inference code, and simulation evaluation suites. Open-HumanWAM-50K is curated and aligned 50,000-hour egocentric pretraining corpus with hand-motion and language annotations, and our experiments demonstrate consistent gains in downstream robot generalization as pretraining on this corpus scales, with out-of-distribution success rates following an empirical log-linear scaling law. The main contributions of this work are as follows: 1. systematic study of egocentric scaling for robot generalization. We present Open-HumanWAM, fully open recipe for scaling pure egocentric pretraining from 100 to 50k hours. We identify an empirical log-linear scaling law in downstream robot task success rates and systematically analyze the benefits of egocentric scaling for robot generalization and adaptation. Building on this recipe, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, which achieves success rates of 92.08% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random after robot post-training, alongside competitive performance on RoboDojo. 2. Emerging robot capabilities through hybrid humanrobot data scaling. With HumanWAM-Goal, we show that scaling joint humanrobot pretraining improves zero-shot task execution in simulation and on physical robots. The model also exhibits embodied in-context learning, adapting its behavior to visual goals without parameter updates. After robot post-training, HumanWAM-Goal achieves state-of-the-art average success rate of 88.65% on RoboTwin 2.0, with 92.70% on Clean2Clean and 84.60% on Clean2Random. 3. full-stack release for reproducible scaling research. We provide the complete resources for reproducing our scaling studies and HumanWAM models. The release includes Open-HumanWAM-50K, curated and aligned 50k-hour egocentric corpus with hand-motion and language annotations, together with training code, model checkpoints and evaluation protocols.

sections.title: 2 Building an Open Egocentric Pretraining Corpus
sections.content: To support systematic scaling studies and large-scale egocentric pretraining, we build Open-HumanWAM-50K, an open corpus from multiple publicly available egocentric datasets (Figure 2). HumanNet [11] is the primary source, contributing egocentric videos collected from the internet and paired with hand-motion and language annotations. We curate manipulation sequences based on hand visibility, motion stability, and manipulation activity. To prepare these heterogeneous sources for joint pretraining, we map action annotations into unified bimanual end-effector representation, aligning camera coordinates, wrist axes, and gripper openness across sources to provide common action interface for subsequent robot adaptation. 4 Figure 2 Construction of Open-HumanWAM-50K. (a) Five data sources and their retained durations. (b) Data curation based on hand visibility, motion stability, and manipulation activity. (c) Cross-source alignment of camera frames, wrist axes, and gripper openness.

sections.title: 2.1 Pretraining Data Sources
sections.content: To support systematic studies of egocentric scaling and large-scale model pretraining, we assemble corpus of 50,000 hours of human manipulation video paired with language descriptions and hand-motion annotations. The corpus combines HumanNet, EgoSuite-Open100K, EgoDex, Gen-HumanEgo, and EgoVerse, which provide egocentric videos with accompanying hand-tracking annotations. Table 1 summarizes the data sources and their scales before and after curation. The corpus contains 31,396,799 physical episodes, which yield 35,934,235 continuous clips after curation, as individual episodes may be split into multiple retained segments. The resulting 35.9 million clips cover broad range of manipulation settings, including household, commercial service, and industrial environments. HumanNet. HumanNet [11] is large-scale human-centric dataset combining one million hours of firstand third-person videos with language and motion annotations. We use an egocentric subset of internet videos covering manipulation, tool use, and multi-step activities across diverse objects and environments. These clips are accompanied by estimated 3D wrist poses, camera trajectories, and LLM-generated captions describing the observed activities and motions. After curation and corpus selection, we retain approximately 40,744 hours for pretraining. EgoSuite-Open100K. EgoSuite-Open100K [75] is large-scale egocentric human activity dataset. It provides head-mounted video synchronized with head-camera poses and tracked hand poses. Each sample includes 21 joint transforms per hand, episode-level task and scene labels, and time-stamped subtask descriptions. The hand annotations support wrist-pose extraction and the estimation of hand openness from fingertip distances, while the task and scene labels enable explicit coverage measurements. We retain 6,358 hours from EgoStandard and 724 hours from EgoPro. 5 Table 1 Source datasets and curation statistics for Open-HumanWAM-50K Dataset Before curation After curation Hours Frames (M) Hours Frames (M) Episodes HumanNet subset [11] EgoSuite-Open100K [75] EgoDex [20] Gen-HumanEgo [17] EgoVerse [43] 90,275.25 11,193.99 829.45 1,847.39 143.33 9,749.73 1,208.95 89.58 199.52 15.48 40,743.58 7,081.65 335.43 1,814.53 24.81 4,400.31 764.82 36.23 195.97 2. 30,833,247 348,724 163,537 44,632 6,659 Total 104,289.41 11,263.26 50,000.00 5,400. 31,396,799 EgoVerse. EgoVerse [43] is continuously expanding collection of egocentric human demonstrations contributed by academic and industrial partners. Its initial release comprises 1,362 hours spanning 1,965 tasks, 240 scenes, and 2,087 demonstrators, combining standardized tasks collected across laboratories with open-ended activities recorded in diverse environments. The data include 3D hand and head poses, camera poses, and language annotations, with fine-grained subtask descriptions for industry-contributed recordings. We use only small subset of the Mecka source, retaining 24.81 hours after curation for Open-HumanWAM-50K. Gen-HumanEgo. Gen-HumanEgo [17] contains over 1,800 hours of human demonstrations across more than 10,000 tasks in domestic, commercial, industrial, and agricultural environments. The dataset provides 21 reconstructed 3D keypoints per hand, MANO [45] parameters, hand meshes, and depth maps. Collected with Apple Vision Pro, it focuses on active manipulation of everyday objects, including dexterous activities such as tying shoelaces and folding laundry. The dataset pairs 30 Hz RGB video with 3D head, upper-body, wrist, and finger poses, camera calibration, and natural-language task descriptions.

sections.title: 2.2 Data Curation
sections.content: Effective large-scale pretraining depends on both corpus scale and supervision quality [34, 66]. We curate egocentric recordings to retain active manipulation with clear visual context and temporally consistent motion annotations. These checks remove unreliable annotations and prolonged inactivity while retaining usable manipulation segments for pretraining. Hand visibility. We assess hand visibility from action annotations to retain manipulation sequences with effective visual context. We project annotated 3D EEF positions into the image using camera calibration to determine whether each end effector lies within the field of view. When only one end effector is in view, we retain the sequence and restrict action supervision to the corresponding hand, excluding the other hand from both the action loss and normalization statistics. Internet videos may also contain incomplete hand views, with only fingers or small portion of hand visible near image boundaries, or excessively close views that limit the visible interaction context. We identify and filter these cases using EEF depth, projected scale, and the location and size of detected hand regions. Action and camera stability. Errors in estimated hand and camera poses can introduce abrupt jumps into manipulation trajectories. For EEF trajectories, we measure differences between original and smoothed positions, together with acceleration, jerk, and changes in position and orientation between adjacent frames. Camera trajectories are checked separately for abrupt pose changes and for excessive displacement or rotation relative to the pose at the start of each chunk. We remove frames that exceed any stability threshold and split sequences at those frames, retaining continuous segments for pretraining. 6 Idle filtering. Long periods of inactivity introduce redundant static samples to the pretraining corpus. We measure EEF positional variation within 32-frame sliding windows and classify window as inactive when this variation is at or below the motion threshold. We trim inactive portions from both ends of each chunk and discard chunks with fewer than 70% active windows.

sections.title: 3 Exploration of Pure Egocentric Data Scaling
sections.content: Egocentric data offer promising route to scaling robot foundation models through abundant and diverse human manipulation experience. Prior work has investigated how pretraining exclusively on human egocentric data affects performance on downstream real-robot tasks [33, 73]. However, scaling outcomes vary across pretraining recipes, with limited or inconsistent downstream generalization gains reported in other settings [50, 56]. We first establish empirical scaling laws for egocentric pretraining with our proposed recipe, then examine data diversity and the sample efficiency of robot adaptation, and finally conduct controlled analyses of the pretraining and adaptation recipe. We organize the scaling analysis around the following questions: Q1. What improves in downstream robot policies as egocentric pretraining scales from 100 to 50k hours? Q2. How important is data diversity for effective egocentric scaling? Q3. How does scaling egocentric pretraining affect the sample efficiency of robot adaptation? Q4. Does cross-source action alignment matter for egocentric pretraining? Q5. Does predicting human motion during egocentric pretraining improve robot action learning? Q6. Can egocentric pretraining surpass robot pretraining at matched data scales? 8 Q7. How do we extend single-view egocentric pretraining to multi-view robot policies?

sections.title: 3.1 Pretraining and Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: To study scaling in pure egocentric pretraining, we adopt unified worldaction model backbone and standardized training and evaluation pipeline (Figure 3). After pretraining on human egocentric data, we adapt each model to RoboTwin 2.0 using clean demonstrations and measure its task success rate in closed-loop evaluation. Standardized tasks and success criteria, controlled environmental variation, and shared evaluation seeds support reproducible comparisons across pretraining scales and training settings. Evaluations within the demonstration distribution and under environmental randomization measure in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization, respectively. Below, we describe the model architecture and the pretraining, robot post-training, and evaluation procedures.

sections.title: 3.1.1 Model.
sections.content: Our experiments build on HumanWAM-Vanilla, worldaction model that jointly generates future video and actions from single observation and language instruction. The model extends Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [53] with an action expert that has the same depth as the video backbone, forming Mixture-of-Transformers architecture. Following prior work [35, 67, 70], we apply widely used isolated attention mask in most experiments, allowing action tokens to attend to the first video frame but not to future video frames. During inference, the model can therefore omit future video generation and denoise only the action chunk, enabling fast policy execution. We use the unified 16-D bimanual end-effector action space defined in Section 2.3 and compute delta poses in the camera coordinate frame relative to the first-frame observation.

sections.title: 3.1.2 Pretraining.
sections.content: We pretrain on different egocentric corpora with the same training recipe. We use the AdamW optimizer [30] with peak learning rate of 104 and weight decay of 0.01. The learning rate follows cosine schedule over 100k steps, with linear warm-up during the first 5% of the steps. The training budget is adapted to the corpus size. In preliminary runs we observed that smaller corpora saturate quickly and that their generalization can even degrade with further training, so fixed budget would either undertrain the large corpora or over-train the small ones. We therefore adjust the global batch size according to the corpus size, as listed in Table 2, and we post-train and evaluate checkpoints saved every 10k pretraining steps so that each corpus is compared at its own best.

sections.content: To assess how egocentric pretraining affects in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization, we evaluate post-trained checkpoints under the clean, scene-ood, and random settings. Each checkpoint is 9 Figure 4 RoboTwin evaluation setup for our egocentric pretraining exploration. We post-train policies exclusively on clean demonstrations and evaluate them under clean, scene-ood, and random conditions. rolled out on all 50 tasks with 50 episodes per task in each setting. Representative tasks and evaluation conditions are illustrated in Figure 4. clean: the training distribution, with the plain background, fixed lighting, no clutter, and fixed table height used to collect the demonstrations. scene-ood: randomized backgrounds and tabletop textures, with all other conditions identical to clean. random: the full RoboTwin randomization, with randomized backgrounds, table clutter, randomized lighting, and table-height jitter of up to 3 cm. Clean measures how well the policy fits the demonstration distribution, whereas scene-ood and random assess gains in downstream generalization from egocentric pretraining. Specifically, scene-ood focuses on robustness to visual scene variation. We find that the post-trained checkpoint with the best clean performance does not necessarily generalize best to randomized scenes. To examine pretraining gains in in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization separately, we therefore report the success rate of the best checkpoint independently for each evaluation setting. To support fair comparisons and accelerate evaluation, we save expert-validated evaluation seeds and reuse them across evaluation rounds.

sections.title: 3.2 Scaling Egocentric Data from 100 to 50k Hours: What Improves?
sections.content: Whether and how scaling human data improves robot policy performance is central question for robot foundation models. We investigate this question through systematic study of egocentric pretraining from 100 to 50,000 hours. Under the same pretraining recipe, we find that scaling egocentric pretraining consistently improves downstream generalization across all three settings. We validate this trend under both isolated attention and inverse-dynamics (IDM) attention, which additionally allows action tokens to attend to the future video. We first examine scaling with isolated attention. Models are pretrained on 100, 500, 1,000, 5,000, and 10,000 hours of egocentric data, then post-trained and evaluated under common downstream protocol. Figure 5 shows that scaling egocentric pretraining with isolated attention consistently improves downstream policy performance on RoboTwin. On clean, success increases from 71.2% at 100 hours to 80.0% at 10,000 hours, compared with 69.5% without egocentric pretraining. These gains indicate improved in-distribution performance under the same post-training protocol. The benefits are larger under distribution shift. From 100 to 10,000 hours, scene-ood success rises from 25.2% to 58.1%, while random success increases from 8.4% 10 to 28.7%. Without egocentric pretraining, the corresponding success rates are only 16.2% and 2.1%. Figure 5 Scaling egocentric pretraining with isolated attention improves in-distribution performance and generalization. Blue dashed lines show least-squares fits of SR = + log10 H, where denotes pretraining hours, with R2 reported in each panel. Gray dashed lines denote the baseline without egocentric pretraining. Success rates increase across all three settings, with larger gains on scene-ood and random, indicating that scaling primarily strengthens generalization beyond the demonstration scenes. Downstream success follows an empirical log-linear scaling law, SR = a+b log10 H, where denotes egocentric pretraining hours. The high goodness of fit (R2 = 0.971, 0.949, and 0.877 for clean, scene-ood, and random, respectively) indicates consistent relationship between pretraining scale and downstream performance. Each tenfold increase in pretraining hours corresponds to fitted gains of 4.43 pp on clean, 15.88 pp on scene-ood, and 10.24 pp on random. These trends suggest that further scaling egocentric pretraining will continue to improve downstream policy performance, with particularly pronounced gains in out-of-distribution generalization. Recent work motivates us to examine whether this scaling trend extends to architectures that condition actions on future visual information. We therefore validate the scaling experiments with inverse-dynamics attention and absolute camera-frame poses, allowing action tokens to attend to both current and future video frames. During training, action denoising is conditioned on the ground truth future video with noise augmentation. During inference, the model first generates future video latents and then predicts actions. This configuration substantially improves downstream performance, with detailed ablations examining the contributions of these design choices in Section 4.4. As shown in Figure 6, clean success remains between 87.4% and 89.0% as egocentric pretraining scales from 100 to 50,000 hours. Even without egocentric pretraining, the model achieves 87.9% on clean, indicating strong in-distribution performance under IDM attention with absolute camera-frame poses. Scaling therefore yields only limited additional gains on the training distribution. The generalization gains are substantially larger. From 100 to 50,000 hours, scene-ood success increases from 49.1% to 73.2%, and random success rises from 21.5% to 42.9%, compared with 29.2% and 7.7% without egocentric pretraining. Improvements persist beyond 5,000 hours, where the corresponding success rates are 62.4% and 32.2%. Both out-of-distribution settings closely follow the empirical log-linear scaling law observed with isolated attention, with higher R2 values of 0.969 for scene-ood and 0.955 for random. This consistency across the two model configurations suggests that the generalization benefits of scaling egocentric pretraining extend beyond specific attention design and action representation, even when in-distribution performance is already strong.

sections.title: 3.3 Scaling Diversity, Not Just Hours
sections.content: Recent studies [14, 33, 73] have explored the scaling behavior of egocentric pretraining, with data duration as the primary scaling variable. Data diversity, including variation in tasks and scenes, is another important dimension of scaling embodied pretraining [27, 47]. We investigate this dimension through controlled experiments on the EgoSuite-Open100K dataset with matched durations but varying task and scene coverage. Our results show that jointly scaling diversity and duration yields greater downstream gains than increasing duration alone. 11 Figure 6 Scaling egocentric pretraining with IDM attention strengthens downstream generalization. Clean success remains high across scales, while scene-ood and random success improve consistently. Blue dashed lines show log-linear scaling fits for the two out-of-distribution settings, with R2 reported in the corresponding panels. Gray dashed lines denote the baseline without egocentric pretraining. Setup. We construct two series of pretraining corpora at 100, 500, 1,000, and 5,000 hours from the EgoSuiteOpen100K dataset. In the scaled-diversity series, task and scene coverage expands with data duration. In the matched-diversity series, the 100-, 500-, and 1,000-hour subsets cover the same set of tasks and scenes as the 5,000-hour parent corpus, so increasing duration adds trajectories within fixed task and scene coverage. At 100 hours, the matched-diversity corpus spans 2,288 tasks and 2,953 scenes, compared with 62 tasks and 222 scenes in the scaled-diversity corpus. For each corpus, we pretrain the model, apply the same post-training protocol, and evaluate success rates under all three settings. The larger slope increases on scene-ood and random suggest that diversity expansion particularly benefits downstream generalization. sections.title: 3.4 Scaling Egocentric Pretraining for Data-Efficient Robot Adaptation
sections.content: Generalization to new tasks and in-context learning have attracted growing interest in embodied pretraining [16, 21, 28]. In this section, we seek to explore how egocentric pretraining scale affects the sample efficiency of downstream robot policy adaptation. 12 Figure 7 Scaling egocentric pretraining with growing or fixed task and scene diversity. Blue circles denote scaled-diversity corpora, and orange squares denote matched-diversity corpora. Dashed and dash-dotted lines show the respective least-squares fits of SR = + log10 H, with both equations shown in each panel. Scaled-diversity yields steeper fitted slope in all three settings. Setup. To assess how egocentric pretraining scale affects the sample efficiency of robot adaptation, we conduct post-training experiments with different initializations and demonstration budgets. We select the best-performing checkpoints from pretraining on 500 and 5,000 hours of egocentric data and compare them with baseline without egocentric pretraining (No-Ego). For each initialization, separate post-training runs use 5, 10, 25, or 50 clean demonstrations per task. Figure 8 Scaling egocentric pretraining improves the sample efficiency of robot adaptation. Success rates as function of the number of robot demonstrations per task for different egocentric pretraining scales. Results. Figure 8 shows consistent scaling trend in post-training sample efficiency. Across all three settings, the 500-hour model outperforms No-Ego at every demonstration budget, with further gains from scaling to 5,000 hours. With 10 demonstrations per task, clean success increases from 34.5% for No-Ego to 44.2% after 500 hours of pretraining and 50.1% after 5,000 hours, indicating progressively more effective adaptation from limited robot demonstrations. At the same budget, scaling from 500 to 5,000 hours also approximately doubles random success, from 4.1% to 8.3%. The additional pretraining therefore improves both in-distribution performance and generalization without requiring more robot demonstrations. These gains also lower demonstration requirements for comparable performance. On scene-ood, the No-Ego success rate with 50 demonstrations per task is exceeded by the 500-hour model with 25 demonstrations and by the 5,000-hour model with only 5. Further scaling from 500 to 5,000 hours continues to reduce dependence 13 on robot demonstrations. With 25 demonstrations, the 5,000-hour model outperforms the 500-hour model trained on 50 demonstrations in both scene-ood (42.0% vs. 37.9%) and random (21.8% vs. 16.2%). This improvement establishes clear scaling trend in post-training sample efficiency, with stronger generalization achieved using half the robot demonstrations.

sections.title: 3.5 Does Cross-Source Action Alignment Matter?
sections.content: Egocentric datasets obtain human action trajectories through different data collection and motion estimation pipelines, producing raw action data that lack consistent physical interpretation across sources. Prior work incorporates geometric alignment to support learning from heterogeneous human and robot data [25, 34, 66]. We quantify the effect of camera-frame and wrist-axis alignment on pretraining loss and downstream policy performance under fixed data mixture and training configuration. Setup. To evaluate the effect of cross-source action alignment, we construct 1,000-hour corpus comprising EgoSuite-Open100K (593.7 h), HumanNet (250 h), EgoDex (114.5 h), and EgoVerse (41.8 h). We compare two models pretrained on identical clips and captions with the same sampling strategy, training schedule, and normalization procedure. In the Aligned setting, actions from each source are transformed into camera coordinates, and wrist axes are standardized to obtain consistent action representation. In the Raw setting, actions from each source are used directly in their original representation. Figure 9 Cross-source action alignment improves downstream policy performance. Aligned and Raw models are pretrained on the same four-source 1,000-hour corpus using aligned and native action representations. Each point reports the best success rate across post-trained checkpoints for the corresponding pretraining run and evaluation setting. Gray dashed lines denote the baseline without egocentric pretraining. Results. Figure 9 shows that Aligned outperforms Raw at every evaluated pretraining step across all three settings. Comparing the best checkpoints, clean success increases from 72.0% to 77.5% (+5.5 pp). The gains are larger under distribution shift, with scene-ood improving from 43.2% to 52.2% and random from 18.0% to 26.4%. Both pretrained models outperform the No-Ego baseline, showing that multi-source pretraining remains beneficial without alignment. Under the same data mixture and training protocol, cross-source action alignment further improves in-distribution performance and, more substantially, out-of-distribution generalization. The effect of action alignment is also evident during pretraining (Figure 10). Aligned exhibits lower action loss, while video loss remains comparable between the two models. These trends suggest that well-aligned action representation provides more consistent supervision across sources and facilitates joint learning.

sections.title: 3.6 Action Supervision in Egocentric Pretraining
sections.content: Egocentric human data capture rich physical interactions in first-person videos paired with hand trajectories [20, 43]. Whether to incorporate human motion prediction into worldaction model pretraining remains an open 14 Figure 10 Cross-source action alignment reduces pretraining action loss with little change in video loss. Curves show training losses for Aligned and Raw models on the same four-source 1,000-hour corpus. question [7, 35, 50, 59]. We show that jointly predicting human motion and future video substantially improves downstream policy generalization over video prediction alone on the same egocentric corpus. Setup. We pretrain two models on the same 1,000-hour scaled-diversity corpus, with and without human motion prediction. For the video-only baseline, we set the action loss weight to zero and optimize video prediction alone. To assess the additional value of human motion targets, we train second model with action loss enabled only for fixed subset of original episodes covering approximately 50% of the total video duration. All models receive full robot action supervision during post-training, following Section 3.1. Figure 11 Human action supervision during egocentric pretraining improves downstream generalization. Models are pretrained on the same 1,000-hour video corpus with 0%, 50%, or 100% human action supervision. Results. Figure 11 shows that learning human motion alongside video prediction consistently improves downstream robot policy performance across all three settings. At 20k pretraining steps, using motion targets for approximately 50% of the video duration increases clean success from 70.4% to 75.2% compared with video-only pretraining. The gains are larger under distribution shift, with scene-ood improving from 13.0% to 34.8% and random from 3.6% to 16.3%. The two objectives also exhibit distinct trends as pretraining progresses. From 10k to 30k steps, video-only performance remains nearly flat, with scene-ood and random success staying near 13% and 3%, respectively. Over the same interval, the model that jointly predicts human motion and future video improves steadily from 30.0% to 40.4% on scene-ood and from 12.3% to 20.1% on 15 Table 4 Composition of the real-robot pretraining corpora. The widening gap indicates that human motion targets improve both performance at matched pretraining steps and the gains in downstream generalization from continued pretraining.

sections.title: 3.7 Can Egocentric Pretraining Surpass Robot Pretraining?
sections.content: Egocentric human data offer broader interaction coverage, greater scene diversity, and higher information density at lower collection cost than teleoperated robot data [33]. To assess their relative value for robot policy learning, HumanScale pretrained models on equal-duration egocentric or real-robot corpora, then post-trained each model on the same real-robot demonstrations. This comparison favored egocentric pretraining, which yielded lower validation action loss on held-out real-robot trajectories, particularly on tasks excluded from post-training. We extend this matched-scale comparison to closed-loop task success on RoboTwin to examine how the relative performance of the two pretraining sources varies with data scale. Setup. We compare egocentric and real-robot pretraining at 100, 500, 1,000, and 5,000 hours. The egocentric series uses the scaled-diversity corpora in Figure 5, while the real-robot series draws on AgiBot Beta [1], ABC-130k [2], and our in-house Cobot Magic data as shown in Table 4. Both series use only head-camera observations during pretraining, given the effects of additional wrist-camera views discussed in Section 3.8. We curate the robot corpora from language-annotated trajectories with verified head-camera extrinsics, excluding data with base or head-camera motion. Figure 12 Egocentric pretraining outperforms robot pretraining from 500 to 5,000 hours. Downstream RoboTwin success rates after pretraining on 100, 500, 1,000, and 5,000 hours of egocentric human or robot data. The egocentric series follows the scaled-diversity configuration in Figure 5. Each point reports the best post-training success rate among the evaluated pretraining checkpoints for that scale and setting. Results. Figure 12 shows that egocentric pretraining outperforms robot pretraining in all three settings from 500 to 5,000 hours. At 100 hours, robot pretraining retains small advantage on scene-ood and random, but this ordering reverses at larger scales. On clean, the egocentric advantage grows from 2.2 pp at 100 hours to 7.3 pp at 5,000 hours. At 5,000 hours, egocentric pretraining also achieves higher out-of-distribution success, reaching 52.3% versus 45.6% on scene-ood and 27.6% versus 22.4% on random. Its advantage therefore spans both in-distribution performance and robustness under distribution shift. The 1,000-hour egocentric model also outperforms the 5,000-hour robot model in all three settings, including scene-ood (48.2% versus 45.6%) 16 and random (25.9% versus 22.4%). These comparisons extend the validation-loss evidence from HumanScale to closed-loop task success on RoboTwin, where egocentric pretraining yields stronger downstream policies despite the embodiment gap.

sections.title: 3.8 From Egocentric Pretraining to Multi-View Robot Policies
sections.content: Most egocentric human data are collected with single head-mounted camera [20, 43]. Although head-camera observations alone can support most robot manipulation tasks, wrist cameras provide complementary closerange views for precise gripperobject interactions and improve visibility when the head view is occluded [23, 71]. We find that introducing wrist-camera inputs directly during robot post-training can substantially damage the generalization benefits of egocentric pretraining. EgoPro [75] provides approximately 1,000 hours of egocentric human video with synchronized headand wrist-camera views. We use this dataset to investigate how to extend egocentric pretraining to multi-view robot policies while preserving its generalization benefits. Figure 13 From egocentric pretraining to multi-view robot policies. Three view configurations and training routes with or without EgoPro mid-training. Multi-view configurations. We compare three configurations for visual conditioning and video prediction, illustrated in Figure 13. Single-view uses the current head-camera observation and predicts future video from the single view. Multi-view conditioning adds current observations from both wrist cameras while restricting future video prediction to the head camera. Multi-view prediction uses the same three-camera inputs and predicts future video for all three views. We evaluate these variants separately under isolated attention with relative EEF actions and IDM attention with absolute camera-frame actions. Within each model configuration, all three variants are post-trained on RoboTwin from the same 20k-step egocentric pretraining checkpoint. Relative to Single-view, scene-ood success falls from 46.1% to 33.034.1% across the two multi-view variants, while random success falls from 22.5% to 12.914.8%. Under IDM attention, Multi-view conditioning improves clean success from 88.5% to 90.6% and maintains comparable random success, while scene-ood success decreases from 62.0% to 59.5%. With the input views unchanged, Multi-view prediction lowers success in all three settings relative to Multi-view conditioning, with scene-ood decreasing from 59.5% to 56.3% and random from 29.1% to 26.2%. Multi-view mid-training. Under IDM attention, both multi-view configurations achieve lower scene-ood success than Single-view after direct robot post-training. We therefore investigate whether mid-training on EgoPro, which provides human egocentric videos with wrist-camera views, can bridge single-view egocentric pretraining and multi-view robot post-training while preserving the generalization gained from human data. For both Multi-view conditioning and Multi-view prediction, we compare this intermediate stage followed by robot post-training with direct post-training from the same pretrained checkpoint, keeping each view configuration fixed across mid-training and robot post-training. Table 5 shows that mid-training improves out-of-distribution performance for both view configurations. With Multi-view conditioning, scene-ood success increases from 59.5% to 61.2% and random success from 29.1% to 30.7%. Multi-view prediction also improves, from 56.3% to 58.8% on scene-ood and from 26.2% to 27.4% on random. Clean success changes little with conditioning and decreases with prediction, so the gains are concentrated in out-of-distribution generalization. After mid-training, Multi-view conditioning approaches Single-view on scene-ood (61.2% versus 62.0%) and exceeds it on random (30.7% versus 28.6%). It also outperforms Multi-view prediction in all three settings, supporting our choice of Multi-view conditioning mid-training before robot post-training.

sections.title: 4 Pure Egocentric Data Foundation Model Training
sections.content: Building on the exploration in Section 3, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, worldaction model pretrained exclusively on 50,000 hours of curated egocentric human data with aligned action trajectories. HumanWAMVanilla achieves competitive performance on the bimanual simulation benchmarks RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo following robot post-training, with strengths in environmental robustness, precise control, and multi-step manipulation. Real-robot experiments further show that egocentric pretraining improves task success over baseline without egocentric pretraining, with particularly large gains under visual distribution shifts.

sections.title:
4.1 Model and Training Setup
Model configuration. HumanWAM-Vanilla follows the world–action architecture described in Section 3.1.1
and uses inverse-dynamics attention, allowing action tokens to attend to both current and future video
frames. During training, action denoising is conditioned on ground-truth future video latents with noise
augmentation. For policy inference, the model first generates future video latents and then predicts an action
chunk conditioned on these latents.
sections.content: Action representation and normalization. We use the unified 16-D bimanual end-effector action space defined in Section 2.3. Each end effector is represented by its three-dimensional position, quaternion orientation, and gripper openness. EEF poses are expressed as absolute poses in the camera frame at the corresponding target time, with camera and wrist axes aligned across sources. Actions and proprioceptive states are standardized using dimension-wise z-score normalization after action alignment. Pretraining statistics are estimated jointly across the curated corpus, while mid-training and robot post-training use statistics estimated from their respective training datasets. Invalid or unsupervised hand dimensions are excluded from both normalization statistics and the action loss. Egocentric pretraining. We pretrain the model exclusively on Open-HumanWAM-50K curated and aligned as described in Section 2, comprising human videos, language annotations, and action trajectories. The action chunk length is 32, and video frames are sampled every four action steps, yielding nine frames per sample. We optimize the model with AdamW [30], setting the global batch size to 8,192 and the weight decay to 0.01. 18 The learning-rate schedule spans 100,000 optimizer steps, with linear warm-up to 104 over the first 5,000 steps followed by cosine decay to 106. Mid-training. After egocentric pretraining with single head-camera view, mid-training adapts the model to multi-view inputs for robot policies. We continue training on EgoPro [75], human egocentric dataset with synchronized video from one head-mounted camera and two wrist-mounted cameras. Under Multi-view conditioning (Section 3.8), current observations from all three cameras condition action prediction, while future video prediction remains restricted to the head camera. Setting RoboTwin 2.0 RoboDojo Real robot Robot demonstrations 2500 3500 50/task Optimizer steps 24,000 50,000 10, Global batch size 512 512 256 Robot post-training. Separate policies are post-trained for RoboTwin 2.0, RoboDojo, and real-robot experiments using the corresponding robot demonstrations. Table 6 summarizes the training data and optimization settings. RoboTwinClean2Clean and RoboTwinClean2Random use the same post-training data, comprising 50 clean demonstrations per task. Robot EEF poses follow the absolute camera-frame representation. Post-training uses AdamW with weight decay of 0.01 and cosine learning-rate schedule preceded by linear warm-up over the first 5% of optimization steps.

sections.title: 4.2 Simulation Experiments
sections.content: Since our egocentric pretraining primarily covers bimanual tabletop manipulation, we evaluate HumanWAMVanilla on RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo. Comparisons with existing visionlanguageaction models and worldaction models assess robustness to environmental variation and capabilities such as precision, memory, and long-horizon execution. RoboTwin 2.0. RoboTwin 2.0 [8] is benchmark built on SAPIEN [60] comprising 50 bimanual tabletop manipulation tasks on the Aloha-AgileX embodiment, including pick-and-place, stacking, object handovers, and articulated-object manipulation. We jointly post-train single policy on clean demonstrations from all tasks and evaluate it in two settings. Clean2Clean evaluates performance within the demonstration environment distribution, whereas Clean2Random randomizes background and tabletop textures, lighting, clutter, and table height. At inference, the policy receives RGB observations from the head camera and both wrist cameras, together with the language instruction and proprioceptive state. It predicts 32-step action chunks and executes the first 24 steps before replanning from updated observations. We evaluate the same checkpoint in both settings, with 100 episodes per task, totaling 5,000 episodes per setting. We report the mean success rate across the 50 tasks in each setting and the average of these two means. Table 7 shows that HumanWAM-Vanilla achieves the highest Clean2Clean success rate among the compared methods, reaching 92.08% after post-training on 50 clean robot demonstrations per task. The same policy achieves 68.88% on Clean2Random, yielding an average success rate of 80.48% that exceeds all VLA baselines and most WAM baselines in the table. The remaining gap to the leading WAMs lies in out-of-distribution performance, with GO-3 Nano Preview reaching 81.48% on Clean2Random. This gap may partly reflect architectural differences, as HumanWAM-Vanilla uses basic worldaction architecture without additional specialized modules. These results support pretraining exclusively on human egocentric data as an effective foundation for bimanual robot manipulation, with accurate task execution and competitive generalization to visual conditions absent from the robot demonstrations. RoboDojo. RoboDojo [9] is an Isaac Sim-based benchmark with 42 bimanual manipulation tasks covering generalization, precision, memory, long-horizon execution, and open-vocabulary instruction following. sections.title: 4.4 Ablation Studies
sections.content: To improve robot policy performance after post-training, we refine the model and training configuration used in the egocentric pretraining exploration. HumanWAM-Vanilla adopts IDM attention and absolute 21 Figure 14 Real-robot tasks and visual evaluation conditions. camera-frame actions in place of the default isolated attention and relative actions described in Section 3.1.1. We examine these choices, together with action-expert initialization, through ablations on the four-source, 1,000-hour corpus described in Section 3.5. All models are pretrained for 20,000 steps and post-trained for 12,000 steps on 50 clean demonstrations per RoboTwin task. Attention strategies. Worldaction models differ in how video and action tokens exchange information. We compare four attention strategies, each applied consistently throughout egocentric pretraining and robot post-training. Isolated attention restricts visual conditioning for action prediction to the current frame. Mutual attention allows video and action tokens to attend to each other during joint denoising. IDM attention conditions action denoising on ground-truth future video latents during training and generated future latents at inference. Optional-IDM, following the variant released by Fast-WAM [15], trains single model to predict actions with or without future video conditioning. Our implementation uses ground-truth future-video conditioning with probability 0.5 and current-frame-only conditioning otherwise. Table 10 shows that mutual and IDM attention improve clean and scene-ood success over isolated attention with relative actions held fixed. Scene-ood success rises from 46.36% to 57.96% and 58.08%, respectively. IDM attention also improves random success from 22.40% to 27.56%. sections.title: 5 Pushing the Model Capability Boundary with Hybrid Data Scaling
sections.content: Scaling pure egocentric pretraining to 50k hours instills strong manipulation priors, substantially improving out-of-distribution generalization after task-specific post-training. However, purely human pretraining leaves an inherent embodiment gap: without exposure to physical robot morphology and control dynamics, the model cannot be deployed directly and remains confined to finetuning paradigm that requires demonstrations for every target task. Conversely, while large-scale robot datasets [58] provide direct, executable control supervision, scaling teleoperated trajectories alone quickly plateaus due to collection cost and limited scene diversity. To overcome these single-modality bottlenecks, we investigate joint co-training on human and robot data within an extended unified action space. Through systematic scaling experiments across progressive human and robot data budgets, we characterize how hybrid data scaling expands the boundary of model generalization and execution capability. 23 central question is whether scaling hybrid training experience reduces reliance on task-specific adaptation. We therefore evaluate our co-trained models across two complementary protocols. In the zero-shot protocol, the pretrained checkpoint is deployed directly in simulation and on physical robots without target-task demonstrations or parameter updates, testing whether larger hybrid budgets expand the repertoire of tasks executable out of the box. In the post-training protocol, the same checkpoints are finetuned on target-task demonstrations, assessing whether hybrid pretraining continues to raise the performance ceiling once in-domain data are available, particularly under out-of-distribution shifts. Deploying generalist policy without task-specific finetuning also requires an unambiguous interface to specify unfamiliar tasks. Because natural language instructions often leave object configurations, spatial relations, and terminal states underspecified, we augment our world-action model with explicit goal-image conditioning [18]. The resulting model, HumanWAM-Goal, jointly predicts future visual states and executable actions from current observations and visual goal. Beyond disambiguating task intent for zero-shot execution, this interface enables embodied in-context learning [28], steering frozen policy toward distinct manipulation outcomes purely by varying the visual goal at inference time. To realize this framework, we first introduce our robot pretraining corpus (Section 5.1), extend the unified action representation (Section 5.2), and detail the HumanWAM-Goal architecture (Section 5.3) alongside its co-training recipe (Section 5.4). We then formalize our evaluation protocols (Section 5.5), examine zero-shot and post-trained scaling trends (Section 5.6), and finally demonstrate emergent zero-shot execution, visual in-context learning, and long-horizon manipulation on physical robots in Section 6.

sections.title: 5.1 Robot Pretraining Data
sections.content: To complement egocentric human experience with embodiment-specific control supervision, we assemble approximately 14.6k hours of robot pretraining data spanning multiple embodiments. The real-robot portion contains over 1.1 million episodes across eight recorded robot domains, providing diverse control experience for cross-embodiment pretraining. Reference frames. While absolute camera-frame EEF poses excel when post-training adapts normalization statistics to single target embodiment (Section 4.4), heterogeneous robot platforms exhibit substantial variations in camera mounting geometry, arm reach, and workspace offsets that impede direct zero-shot transfer. To eliminate these embodiment-specific spatial biases during multi-domain co-training and zero-shot deployment, we parameterize EEF motions as chunk-relative displacements anchored to the current observation. Specifically, given an observation at time t, EEF translation targets at each chunk step τ are expressed as displacements from the current EEF position projected into the anchor head-camera frame at time t, p(τ t) = RH (t)(p(τ ) p(t)), ensuring stationary, embodiment-agnostic reference frame across the entire chunk even under camera motion. Hybrid supervision and joint dropout. Human and robot trajectories share common input and output projections for the 16-D EEF and 3-D chassis subspaces, whereas jt uses embodiment-specific projections. Per-source validity masks exclude unavailable dimensions (such as joints and chassis in human videos) from the action loss. During robot training, we additionally apply stochastic dropout to the joint branch jt, preventing the model from over-relying on embodiment-specific joint proprioception and ensuring that the shared 16-D EEF pathway remains self-sufficient. Because at parameterizes camera-frame metric displacements and physical gripper widths in an embodiment-agnostic coordinate frame, its global pretraining normalization statistics transfer directly to unseen robots at test time without target-domain recalibration.

We therefore introduce HumanWAM-Goal (Figure 16), which augments world-action modeling with explicit visual-goal conditioning [18]. We build HumanWAM-Goal upon the pretrained Cosmos3-Nano-16B backbone [38], which pairs frozen Qwen3-VL-based Reasoner for language encoding with shared video-action Generator. Visual goal and observation conditioning. To enable unambiguous task specification without modifying the backbone topology, all visual inputs are encoded into spatial latents via frozen Wan VAE and mapped into the Generator through shared visual projection . While the current observation ot serves as the clean anchor frame of the rollout, the goal image is encoded separately, augmented with learnable goal embedding, and supplied as clean conditioning tokens. This design preserves the fine-grained spatial structure of the desired outcome while distinguishing goal targets from current observations. When historical frames Ht are included, they enter as additional clean visual tokens with temporal rotary position embeddings (RoPE) reflecting their elapsed time relative to ot. Specifically, video and action tokens share Transformer weights and interact bidirectionally at every denoising step through joint self-attention via modality-specific projections i/o . At inference, holding all conditioning tokens ct fixed, the Generator synchronously denoises future video latents and the 48-step action chunk via and i/o 26 iterative UniPC updates, preserving world-to-action coupling while halving sampling latency and optionally bypassing the Wan VAE decoder for real-time control.

sections.title:
5.4 Training Recipe
Training data. We investigate human–robot data scaling through two complementary series. In the robot-only
series, we progressively expand the robot training corpus from 2,005 to 14,618 hours (2,005 / 4,261 / 8,475 /
14,618 hours), drawn from eight real-world robot domains (Section 5.1). In the hybrid series, we hold the
robot corpus fixed at 14,618 hours and incorporate either 15,901 or 45,938 hours of egocentric human data
drawn from the curated corpus in Section 2.1, yielding total training budgets of approximately 30.5k and
60.6k hours, respectively. This design isolates the benefits of scaling robot demonstrations from the additional
contribution of human experience at a fixed robot-data budget. Both modalities are represented in the unified
action space described in Section 5.2.
sections.content: Goal images. During co-training, goal images are sampled online from future observations within the same trajectory using an identical strategy for human and robot data. For each training example, we sample clean head-camera frame from four goal-conditioning options: future observation 28 ahead (40%), the episodes terminal observation (20%), the final observation of an upcoming annotated subtask (20%), or an empty goal (20%). Goal timestamps are constrained to lie at or beyond the end of the supervised action chunk. Each goal image is encoded with learnable goal embedding and serves exclusively as conditioning signal without an associated reconstruction loss. When the goal is omitted, its tokens are removed entirely, enabling single model to support both goal-conditioned and language-only execution. Optimization. All configurations start from the same pretrained Cosmos3-Nano-16B initialization. We optimize the Generator, timestep embeddings, visual and action projections, action modality embedding, and goal embedding, while keeping the Reasoner and VAE frozen. Training uses FusedAdam with base learning rate of 4 105, (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.99), weight decay of 0.05, gradient-norm clipping at 1.0, and global batch size of 1,024. The learning rate increases linearly over the first 1,000 steps and subsequently decays linearly over 500k-step schedule. We apply 5 learning-rate multiplier to the action projections, action modality embedding, and goal embedding. All evaluations use exponential moving average (EMA) weights. RoboTwin post-training. For simulation evaluation, we initialize from the co-trained checkpoint and adapt the model using 50 clean demonstrations from the ALOHA-AgileX robot per RoboTwin task, totaling 2,500 trajectories. Table 12 summarizes the adaptation protocols used in our post-training scaling and leaderboard evaluations (Section 5.6.2). Action normalization statistics are computed jointly from the clean RoboTwin datasets and pretraining data. For goal specification during post-training, we use mixture of ground-truth terminal frames and synthesized goal images. Specifically, 20% of the training episodes use the ground-truth terminal observation as the goal, while the remaining 80% use goal images synthesized by GPT Image 2.5 [40]. Each goal image is generated from the initial scene observation and task instruction using fixed task-specific prompt (Appendix A). To ensure fidelity to the intended task, every generated image undergoes an automated review using ChatGPT Astra High [39], which verifies the target object and destination, designated manipulation arm, object count and appearance, and background and viewpoint consistency. Images that fail any check are regenerated and reviewed until accepted; this procedure enforces visual and instructional consistency rather than physical feasibility. At evaluation time, each scene is assigned single generated goal image shared across all evaluated checkpoints to eliminate goal variation as source of performance differences.

sections.title:
5.5 Evaluation Settings
Benchmark. To ensure reproducibility and fair comparison with existing robot policies, we adopt RoboTwin
2.0 [8], a standardized simulation benchmark for bimanual manipulation. Built on the SAPIEN physics engine,
RoboTwin 2.0 provides 50 manipulation tasks with predefined success criteria and controlled environmental
variations. We evaluate all models using the ALOHA-AgileX embodiment, which is never exposed during
pretraining. During each episode, the policy receives visual observations, robot states, and task instructions,
executing actions in closed loop. Task success is determined by the benchmark’s automated, task-specific
completion checks.
sections.content: 27 RoboTwin 2.0 defines two evaluation conditions: Clean, which uses the default scene configuration, and Random, which introduces variations in backgrounds, lighting, object clutter, and table height. Together, they assess task execution under standard conditions and robustness to environmental shifts across the same 50 tasks and identical success criteria. Evaluation protocols. We consider two complementary protocols to disentangle the capabilities acquired during co-training from those gained through target-task adaptation  (Table 12)  . In the zero-shot protocol, co-trained checkpoints are deployed directly on RoboTwin 2.0 without any target-task demonstrations or parameter updates, testing whether scaling hybrid experience enables unseen manipulation tasks to be executed out of the box. In the post-training protocol, each co-trained checkpoint is adapted using 50 Clean demonstrations per task to evaluate how pretraining scale affects downstream in-domain fit and out-ofdistribution generalization. For computational efficiency, zero-shot evaluations use 50 episodes per task under each condition (Clean and Random), whereas post-training scaling and leaderboard evaluations follow the official protocol of 100 episodes per task and condition (10,000 episodes in total). To characterize the breadth of zero-shot execution beyond aggregate success rates, we also report task coverage, defined as the number of tasks achieving at least 2% mean success across Clean and Random (corresponding to at least two successful rollouts out of 100 episodes). sections.title: 6 Emerging Capabilities in Real-World Robot Behavior
sections.content: While recent multimodal agents exhibit strong high-level reasoning and task planning [28, 48], translating semantic intent into physical work requires general-purpose action executor that can reliably control real robots. Building on the simulation scaling trends in Section 5which show that joint humanrobot co-training with visual-goal conditioning instills transferable visuomotor priorswe transition to physical hardware to evaluate whether HumanWAM-Goal can bridge this gap. Central to our deployment is explicit goal-image conditioning, which decouples high-level task specification from low-level sensorimotor control. Rather than relying solely on language instructions that often leave spatial arrangements and terminal states underspecified, an upstream planner or user supplies visual goal as inference-time context. This unified interface allows the model to serve both as an out-of-the-box executor for unseen tasks and as scalable foundation for downstream post-training. Following our experimental setup (Section 6.1), we evaluate the real-world behaviors of HumanWAM-Goal across three core capabilities. First, we investigate zero-shot real-world manipulation (Section 6.2) by deploying co-trained checkpoints directly across 20-task benchmark, quantifying how hybrid humanrobot scaling expands the set of skills executable without target-task demonstrations or parameter updates. Second, we examine embodied in-context learning (Section 6.3), testing whether policy with strictly frozen weightsboth before and after post-trainingcan dynamically alter its manipulation trajectory in response to varying robotor human-depicted visual goals. Finally, we demonstrate long-horizon execution (Section 6.4) on post-trained policies, showcasing temporal continuity and subgoal chaining across extended, multi-stage tabletop and mobile-manipulation workflows.
