We retain the co-training normalization statistics and recalculate only channels with substantially shifted distributions (e.g., the articulated torso of Astribot S1). During post-training, goal images are sampled online from the final frame of one of the next two annotated subtasks, future frame within 4 s, or an empty goal. To improve robustness and enforce reliance on visual goals and shared EEF representations, we apply 20% dropout to the joint-state input branch, 10% dropout to language instructions, and weight the action loss 10 relative to the video prediction loss. We select the EMA checkpoint that minimizes end-effector average displacement error (ADE) on held-out validation episodes.

sections.title: 6.2 Real-World Zero-Shot Performance
sections.content: We evaluate the zero-shot transfer of HumanWAM-Goal on physical hardware by comparing the robot-only baseline (14, 618 h) against hybrid checkpoints co-trained with an additional 15, 901 or 45, 938 hours of egocentric human data (yielding total budgets of 30, 519 and 60, 556 h, respectively). All checkpoints are deployed directly out of the box without target-task demonstrations or parameter updates. Figure 20 Zero-shot real-robot performance stratified by task difficulty. Success rates across easy and hard tasks as egocentric human data are added to fixed 14, 618 robot corpus. The vertical dashed line at 60, 556 highlights the additional gain on hard tasks from robot-balanced batch sampling (+8 pp). Scaling trends across task difficulty. Figure 20 illustrates how scaling hybrid data affects real-world zero-shot execution across different task difficulties. As egocentric human data expand from 0 to 15.9k and 45.9k hours, success on easy tasks rises steadily from 32.0% to 34.0% and 42.0% (+10.0 pp overall), while success on hard tasks more than doubles from 8.0% to 18.0% and 19.0% (+11.0 pp). These consistent gains confirm that visuomotor priors learned from human manipulation transfer directly to physical robot execution. Notably, while easy tasks benefit most when scaling from 30.5k to 60.6k total hours, gains on hard tasks begin to plateau under standard data-proportional sampling, where human clips constitute roughly 76% of the training mixture. To test whether this plateau stems from diluted embodiment-specific supervision, we evaluate robot-balanced configuration at the 60.6k-hour scale that enforces 1:1 ratio of robot and human samples in every training batch. Holding the data budget fixed, robot-balanced sampling boosts hard-task success from 19.0% to 27.0% (+8.0 pp). This result indicates that while massive human data provide broad interaction priors, preserving sufficient batch exposure to robot trajectories is crucial for executing more demanding multi-step or precision-critical skills. Task-level analysis and coverage expansion. Figure 21 breaks down zero-shot performance across all 20 benchmark tasks. Under the standard scaling series, overall mean success across the 20 tasks increases monotonically from 20.0% (robot-only) to 26.0% (+15.9k human) and 30.5% (+45.9k human). Partial task completion improves in tandem, with the macro-averaged progress score rising from 2.535 to 3.365 and 4.205 out of 10. Equally important, hybrid scaling expands real-world task coverage: the number of tasks Figure 21 Per-task zero-shot evaluation on physical robots. Task-level success rates (left) and mean progress scores (right) across all 20 benchmark tasks for the robot-only baseline and three humanrobot hybrid configurations. achieving at least one successful zero-shot rollout increases from 10/20 with robot-only pretraining to 14/20 and 16/20 as human experience is incorporated. Echoing our simulation findings (Section 5.6.1), human data not only refine reliability on already feasible skillssuch as Grasp and shake bottle (60% 90%) and Place block on tray (10% 50%)but also unlock entirely new capabilities where the robot-only baseline never succeeds (0%), including Stack blocks (30%), Arrange blocks (20%), and Lift one bottle with each hand (30%). Examining the per-task breakdown for the 60.6k-hour robot-balanced model further clarifies its advantage on hard manipulation tasks. Compared with unweighted sampling at the same scale, balancing the humanrobot ratio substantially improves tasks that require precise spatial alignment or bimanual coordinationsuch as Put glue stick in pen holder (10% 40%), Stack two bowls (0% 60%), and Lift one bottle with each hand (30% 60%). By preventing the large human corpus from overwhelming embodiment-specific control dynamics, balanced co-training effectively combines human-scale visual-semantic diversity with high-precision robotic execution. Qualitative analysis of zero-shot rollouts. Figure 22 visualizes representative zero-shot rollouts across eight real-world tasks. Beyond matching the terminal object arrangement depicted in the goal image, the policy exhibits purposeful intermediate behaviors that are not explicitly specified in the static visual goalsuch as reorienting pen holder prior to inserting glue stick (row e) and coordinating both arms to swap or distribute objects without collision (rows b, f, h). These qualitative trajectories complement our quantitative metrics, demonstrating that HumanWAM-Goal translates static goal context into coherent, multi-step physical interactions out of the box.

sections.title: 6.3 In-Context Learning with Visual Goals
sections.content: Whereas Section 6.2 evaluates whether pretrained capabilities transfer directly to unseen tasks, we now examine complementary question: can single policy with strictly frozen parameters dynamically alter its execution trajectory when the desired outcome is modified purely through inference-time visual context? We evaluate this form of embodied in-context learning (ICL) by conditioning the same checkpoint on alternative 34 Figure 22 Qualitative real-robot zero-shot rollouts. Each row pairs the inference-time goal image (left) with four head-camera keyframes from the resulting zero-shot execution (right), showing the initial scene, two intermediate interaction stages, and the final state. The examples span object transport and placement, coordinated bimanual manipulation, object reordering, and multi-step tool/container interactions. 35 goal images from identical initial scenesvarying target locations, category-to-container assignments, or stacking orders. We first verify that goal-responsive behavior emerges directly from co-training, then show that it scales to complex, multi-decision workflows after task-specific post-training, and finally demonstrate cross-embodiment ICL using egocentric human goal images. Pretrained HumanWAM-Goal in-context learning behavior. We first probe visual goal conditioning in the co-trained checkpoint without any target-task post-training. Figure 23 compares two rollouts initialized from the same tabletop scene containing colored blocks, conditioned on visual goals that specify distinct destinations for bottle. Keeping all policy weights fixed, switching the goal image steers the robot to place the bottle either on the tabletop in front of the green block (panel a) or atop the elevated purple block (panel b). While fine-grained release stability on the elevated block remains imperfect without task-specific adaptation, these rollouts confirm that spatial goal grounding is already present out of the box after hybrid pretraining. Figure 23 Visual goal conditioning in pretrained HumanWAM-Goal. Each panel pairs the inference-time goal image (left) with synchronized first-person and third-person keyframes (right). Without target-task post-training or parameter updates, changing the visual goal directs the policy to place the bottle (a) on the tabletop in front of the green block or (b) atop the large purple block. In-context learning behavior after post-training. We next evaluate whether goal-conditioned steerability is preservedand extended to multi-step, compositional decisionsafter adapting the co-trained checkpoint on task-specific demonstrations. Crucially, once post-training concludes, policy parameters remain frozen across all evaluations; behavioral changes arise solely from the supplied goal image. Figure 24 evaluates post-trained policy on multi-object tabletop organization task under three distinct visual goals. Rather than memorizing single canonical sorting routine, the frozen policy parses multiple compositional constraints from the goal image within each rollout: it reverses category-to-bin assignments when the destinations of toy cars and plush toys are swapped (panel vs. panel b), and it modifies both the stacking order (green vs. purple book on top) and the spatial placement of the book stack when prompted by panel c. Visual goal conditioning thus scales beyond single-target localization to coordinate multiple object-level decisions over extended manipulation horizons. Figure 25 further tests paired goal variations in an office workspace involving articulated storage and multi-item sorting. In panels (a, b), the visual goal dictates which drawer of cabinet holds tape roll and tape measure; to satisfy the goal, the policy selectively pulls open either the upper or the middle drawer before inserting 36 Figure 24 Goal-based in-context learning after post-training for tabletop sorting and stacking. Each panel pairs supplied goal image (left, blue border) with eight chronological third-person frames (right, read left-to-right across the top then bottom row; green border marks the final state). The goals specify (a) sorting toy cars into the blue bin, plush toys into the white bin, and stacking books near the table center with the green book on top; (b) swapping the toy-to-bin assignments; and (c) retaining the original toy assignments while placing the purple book on top of stack shifted toward the white bin. 37 Figure 25 Goal-based in-context learning after post-training for office desk organization. Each panel pairs goal image and enlarged detail view (left) with six ordered third-person execution frames (right). Panels (a, b) redirect the storage of tape roll and tape measure from the upper drawer to the middle drawer. Panels (c, d) swap the destinations of glue stick and two pens between the left and right holders (defined in the goal-image frame). Endpoints show item placement prior to drawer closure in (a, b) and after the final pen release in (c, d). 38 both items. In panels (c, d), swapping the visual arrangement of glue stick and two pens between adjacent holders prompts the robot to invert its placement sequence accordingly. These comparisons demonstrate that post-trained policies remain tightly conditioned on visual context, even when realizing the target state requires prerequisite interactions with articulated mechanisms. Cross-embodiment in-context learning from human goal images. Because HumanWAM-Goal is co-trained on heterogeneous human and robot corpora within unified visuomotor framework, we hypothesize that it learns an embodiment-agnostic representation of scene structure and manipulation outcomes. To test this hypothesis directly, we supply the post-trained robot policy with egocentric human goal imagesin which human hands, rather than robot grippers, are visible alongside the desired object configurationand evaluate whether the robot can ground and execute the specified arrangement without parameter updates. As shown in Figure 26, despite the visual domain gap and the presence of human hands in the conditioning images, the policy accurately interprets the underlying spatial relations and adapts its execution across both paired comparisons: it slots the brown notebook into either the rightmost or leftmost compartment before arranging the white notebooks (panels vs. b), and it caps the mug before transporting it to either the monitor or the file rack (panels vs. d). These results are consistent with the hypothesis that humanrobot co-training facilitates the transfer of goal semantics across embodiments.

sections.title: 6.4 Long-Horizon Execution
sections.content: While the paired-goal comparisons in Section 6.3 isolate immediate responsiveness to visual context, real-world deployment often requires chaining diverse manipulation skills over extended horizons. In such settings, each action alters the scene state for subsequent subgoals, requiring the policy to transition smoothly across subtasks without disturbing previously completed arrangements. We evaluate HumanWAM-Goal after task-specific post-training across two representative long-horizon workflows: multi-stage desk organization within shared tabletop workspace and mobile household tidying across multiple work areas. Multi-stage tabletop organization. Figure 27 illustrates continuous 14-stage rollout on cluttered office desk. Across the trajectory, the policy coordinates distinct manipulation primitivescapping and relocating mug (stages 0103), sorting small stationery into holders (0405), opening and closing two separate drawers to store tape roll and tape measure (0610), and filing notebooks into vertical rack (1114). Because all operations unfold within confined workspace, later actions must navigate around earlier placements: the capped mug remains undisturbed near the monitor, and closed drawers stay shut while the robot manipulates adjacent objects. This rollout demonstrates coherent skill chaining across rigid-object placement, container insertion, and articulated-object manipulation. Multi-area mobile household tidying. Figure 28 extends evaluation from stationary tabletop to room-scale mobile manipulation on Astribot S1. Within single uninterrupted sequence, the policy sorts toys into bins and stacks books at the main table (keyframes 0108), navigates to side table to collect and discard two plastic bottles into waste bin (0915), traverses to two chairs to gather deformable garments into laundry hamper (1627), and finally returns to the organized tabletop (28). By coupling base navigation with bimanual control in the unified 49-D hybrid action space (Section 5.2), the model transitions seamlessly across spatial zones and object modalitiesfrom rigid toys and bottles to deformable clothing. Together, these demonstrations show that HumanWAM-Goal can sustain temporally consistent, multi-skill execution across both dense tabletop layouts and extended mobile-manipulation workflows.

sections.title: 7.1 World Action Models
sections.content: Worldaction models couple visual dynamics prediction with action generation, allowing robot policies to inherit manipulation priors from pretrained video models [57, 65]. DreamZero [65] learns control through joint videoaction modeling, while LingBot-VA [26] integrates frame prediction and policy execution within an autoregressive diffusion framework. The role of future visual information in action prediction remains an important architectural consideration [56, 70]. Fast-WAM [67] retains video prediction during training but omits future video generation during inference. OpenWAM [56] systematically studies worldaction 39 Figure 26 Cross-embodiment in-context learning from egocentric human goal images. Each panel pairs human-demonstrated goal image and enlarged detail view (left, showing human hands) with synchronized first-person and third-person robot execution frames (right). Panels (a, b) direct the robot to file the brown notebook into the rightmost or leftmost rack slot, respectively. Panels (c, d) specify placing the covered mug near the monitor or beside the file rack. Green borders highlight the completed placements upon gripper release. 40 Figure 27 Long-horizon desk organization with HumanWAM-Goal. Fourteen chronologically ordered stages from single continuous rollout, shown through paired first-person (left) and third-person (right) views. The trajectory sequentially executes mug capping and placement, pen and glue-stick sorting, articulated drawer storage of tape roll and tape measure, and notebook filing. Green borders mark the terminal state after the final notebook is released into the rack. Figure 28 Long-horizon mobile household tidying with HumanWAM-Goal. Twenty-eight chronologically ordered keyframes from single continuous rollout spanning multiple work areas: sorting tabletop toys and books, navigating to side table to collect and discard empty bottles, gathering garments from two chairs into laundry hamper, and returning to the main table. 42 information flow and embodied pretraining, demonstrating the benefits of explicit world-to-action interaction and synchronized joint denoising. InternW0- [34] instead uses training-only future supervision to learn predictive representations for action generation without video rollout during inference. Extending worldaction modeling to compositional manipulation, ViGAR [18] combines visual subgoal planning with goal-conditioned execution. Our work complements these architectural developments by studying the effects of egocentric data scaling across different worldaction configurations.

sections.title: 7.2 Pure Egocentric Pretraining
sections.content: Pretraining on human manipulation provides visual representations and action priors for robot learning before embodiment-specific adaptation [22, 36]. Being-H0 [31] develops human-motion pretraining for dexterous manipulation, while EgoScale [73] scales action-labeled egocentric pretraining to over 20,000 hours and reports log-linear relationship between data scale and validation loss. EgoScale subsequently introduces aligned humanrobot mid-training to facilitate embodiment transfer. HumanScale [33] establishes an empirical scaling law relating egocentric pretraining hours to validation action loss after robot post-training and finds that human data can outperform robot data at matched pretraining durations. Dyna-2 [14] extends human-video pretraining to one million hours, reporting scaling in zero-shot action prediction on unseen robot data alongside improvements in post-trained robot task performance. Building on these findings, Open-HumanWAM systematically evaluates egocentric scaling through closed-loop policy success under both in-distribution and out-of-distribution conditions. Beyond data duration, our controlled comparisons establish diversity as an additional scaling dimension and quantify gains in the sample efficiency of robot adaptation.

sections.title: 7.3 Zero-Shot Generalization and In-Context Learning
sections.content: Generalist robot policies increasingly extend beyond task-specific adaptation toward direct execution in unfamiliar tasks, environments, and embodiments [21, 65]. Contextual guidance provides complementary mechanism for specifying unfamiliar behaviors without task-specific parameter updates. π0.7 [42] incorporates language, behavioral metadata, and visual subgoals into multimodal prompts, enabling compositional generalization and flexible control over task execution. Demonstration-based in-context learning additionally conditions behavior on examples and interaction history [16, 28]. RoboICL [28] combines demonstration context with accumulated interaction memory while keeping model parameters fixed. Our HumanWAM-Goal experiments connect these capabilities to the scale of human experience. With robot training data held fixed, we quantify the effect of increasing egocentric data on zero-shot robot performance and qualitatively evaluate visual-goal conditioning before and after robot post-training.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented Open-HumanWAM, fully open recipe for scaling robot learning with egocentric human experience. Our study of pure egocentric pretraining from 100 to 50,000 hours reveals an empirical log-linear scaling law in downstream out-of-distribution success. Expanding task and scene diversity strengthens this scaling trend, while larger-scale pretraining improves the sample efficiency of robot adaptation. Controlled experiments further demonstrate the value of human motion prediction and cross-source action alignment. Following this recipe, HumanWAM-Vanilla achieves competitive performance in simulation and improved robustness to visual distribution shifts on physical robots after robot post-training. Our release of annotated data, training code, checkpoints, and evaluation protocols provides reproducible foundation for further research on egocentric scaling. HumanWAM-Goal extends this exploration to joint humanrobot co-training with visual-goal conditioning, improving zero-shot transfer in simulation and achieving state-of-the-art average success on RoboTwin 2.0. On physical robots, hybrid scaling with robot-balanced sampling boosts zero-shot success and expands task coverage without target-task demonstrations. Visual goals also enable embodied in-context learning with frozen parameters, steering policies across spatial and compositional variations as well as cross-embodiment human goal images after post-training. Finally, post-trained policies support coherent subgoal chaining across long-horizon desk organization and room-scale mobile household tidying.

sections.title: A Prompts for Goal Image Synthesis and Review
sections.content: RoboTwin provides no reference goal images, so we synthesize one head-camera goal image for each scene. The only scene-specific inputs are the initial head-camera observation and the task instruction; no expert trajectory, terminal frame, or simulator state is used. Synthesis has two stages: grounding stage localizes the taskrelevant objects in the initial image, and an editing stage turns the initial observation into completed-task observation. Each newly generated evaluation goal image is then reviewed and, if necessary, repaired. A.1 Pipeline Overview Inputs and resolution. The initial head image is letterboxed to 288224 pixels (widthheight) and upsampled 4 to 1152896 for upload. GPT Image 2.5 generates 1152896 image at medium quality, which we downsample to 288224 before restoring the original black letterbox pixels. The editing request contains three images: (1) the upsampled initial head view, (2) task-independent robot appearance sheet, and (3) pixel-registered overlay of the initial view that marks the grounded objects. Task-specific reference annotations. For each of the 50 RoboTwin tasks, we manually wrote one reference annotation on reference scene. It lists the objects (identifier, description, bounding box, and whether the object moves or stays fixed), natural-language description of the required final state, and visual acceptance checks. few tasks also include optional geometric guides: hinge anchor lines for articulated objects, finalextent outlines, relocation cut-outs, or edit masks. These 50 annotations are fixed across all experiments; Stage 1 adapts them to each new scene. A.2 Stage 1: Scene-Specific Grounding For new scene, reasoning model (GPT-5.5, high reasoning effort) adapts the tasks reference annotation to the current initial image and returns structured JSON with fixed schema. Its inputs are the reference initial image, the current initial image, copy of the current image overlaid with pixel-coordinate grid, the reference instruction and annotation, the current instruction, and RoboTwins public task description. The prompt template is: Adapt an initial-scene annotation to DIFFERENT seed of the same RoboTwin task. Return JSON only. Image 1 is the reference seeds INITIAL head view. Image 2 is the CURRENT seeds INITIAL head view. Image 3 is exactly the current initial view with coordinate grid and rulers labelled in NATIVE pixels. No image is completed task. Images 1 and 2 are enlarged 4x from 288x224 native canvas. ALL output coordinates must use native 288x224 pixels. Use Image 3s numbered grid to locate each edge accurately, then confirm on Image 2. Do not estimate coordinates from resized display: interpolate the supplied ruler numbers. Identify actual current object instances, including distractors. Adapt every object description, box, arm, color, source/destination, number, direction and numeric coordinate in the plan and checks to Image 2 and CURRENT INSTRUCTION. Do NOT copy reference coordinates, scene sides, colors or asset names blindly. Use the references correction principles, not its seed-specific scene geometry. Only explicitly manipulated objects are fixed=false; distractors are fixed=true. Preserve its physical task semantics and minimal-change rules. In an ambiguous noun (container/object), select the current instance matching the instruction, not an unrelated colorful distractor. If instruction names objects or arms, those names take precedence over the reference plan. Some benchmark instructions mention ONLY THE FIRST SUBSTEP (for example grab the red block for handover_block). The TASK ID and references complete final-state plan still specify the whole task: preserve the transfer and final placement, not merely that first grab. Do not drop the final task relation because an abbreviated instruction omits it. Ground solely in initial RGB, instruction and the example. Do not infer hidden simulator poses, consult future states, or fabricate an observed terminal image. Keep the same context method: registered initial labels; stationary anchors for articulated devices; proposed final extents only when the reference has those; unscaled initial-pixel relocation guides only when the reference has those; edit masks only when the reference has those. Empty arrays for unused features. Objects may differ in count/identity between seeds. Tight boxes must cover actual visible objects. Coordinates are integer pixels within x=0..288, y=0..224. Bounds [x0,y0,x1,y1] have positive width/height. Point coordinates use x=0..287,y=0..223. No more than 16 objects. 49 For hinged devices, mark the ACTUAL stationary base edge/corners and original hinge from Image 2, not an axis-aligned imagined laptop. Rotate only the lid/door about that hinge. Preserve existing plain surfaces, never add keyboard. For relocation guides trace tight polygon around the COMPLETE current target silhouette in Image 2; propose an integer translation [dx,dy] placing that same unscaled silhouette on the actual support. Do not include unrelated object or large background areas in the cutout. Destination is the usable platform, not its display/handle. Keep the fixed support unchanged; natural overhang is okay. Masks must include the WHOLE source, whole destination silhouette and margin for contact/shadows; avoid editing unrelated background. All dimensions/diagonal yaw remain those in Image 2. For goals requiring rotation or changing orientation, use final extent outlines rather than translation that contradicts the task. For stacking, preserve dimensions and ordering specified in current instruction. Write plan and acceptance_checks with current coordinates if helpful. Annotations are proposals from initial pixels; never describe them as ground truth. TASK: {task} REFERENCE INSTRUCTION: {reference_instruction} REFERENCE ANNOTATION JSON: {reference_annotation} CURRENT INSTRUCTION (authoritative for named instances/arms): {instruction} {public_task_block} The placeholder {public_task_block} is the same public-task block that closes the Stage-2 prompt below. It contains RoboTwins public task description and placeholder schema, followed by few lines of reviewed qualitative guidance for the task. A.3 Stage 2: Goal Image Editing The editing prompt for GPT Image 2.5 is fixed template filled with the current instruction and the Stage-1 output ({objects}, {plan}, and {acceptance_checks}). Paragraphs marked with bracketed tag are included only for tasks whose reference annotation provides the corresponding guide. Gray italic text is explanatory and is not part of the prompt. Edit Image 1 into ONE successful terminal HEAD-CAMERA observation of this exact simulated robot scene. IMAGE ROLES: 1. Initial head view: authoritative camera, framing, geometry, appearance and scene layout. 2. Robot appearance sheet: robot construction only; its poses/background are not task targets. 3. REGISTERED geometry overlay: exactly the same initial head image at exactly the same pixel coordinates and scale as Image 1. Magenta boxes identify movable objects; cyan boxes/lines anchor fixed objects or base edges. The boxes are initial identity bounds, NOT requested object sizes or final locations. All annotations are explanatory only: output NO text, boxes, panels or arrows. INSTRUCTION: {instruction} GROUNDED INITIAL OBJECTS (pixel boxes use Image 1s 288x224 coordinates): {objects} (expands to one line per object: - ID: description; initial box [x0, y0, x1, y1].) REQUIRED FINAL STATE: {plan} CONSERVATION RULES: Apply the smallest physical change that satisfies the final state. Preserve camera extrinsics/intrinsics, table, background, light, object identities/materials/scale, every distractor, and fixed destination geometry. Translate/rotate only explicitly movable objects. Preserve exact object count; remove moved objects from their old locations. Reconstruct only newly exposed surfaces, with the existing simulator style. Do not canonicalize, beautify, replace or enlarge objects to improve visibility. broad/awkward noun in the instruction refers to the specifically identified visible object above. For articulated tasks, preserve the stationary bodys original projected corners and yaw. Rotate only the moving part around its existing hinge; never swivel the whole device toward the viewer. For press, retain the devices position and orientation and show the requested arms gripper contacting the actual control specified by the current instruction. control may face sideways; do not add top button or rotate the device to expose it. For hold/lift, show real grasp with clearance above the support; for place/stack, show supported objects at the destination; release only grasps no longer required by the public complete task, and retain required support-holding grasps. Preserve the two-arm robots construction, connected kinematic chains and plausible reach. An idle arm can stay outside the head frame. Do not invent extra hands/arms or use floating disconnected gripper. Before rendering, mentally match each ID to its original instance, distinguish movable and fixed parts, and check count, final relation, support/contact and stationary edges. Occlusion is natural: do not move fixed objects or change the camera just to reveal them. Output only the completed scene, at the exact aspect ratio and padding of Image 1. No goal image or future state is provided. GEOMETRY PRIORITY: Image 1 is already the requested 1152x896 output size. Edit it in place: preserve unedited pixels and their exact coordinates. Image 3 aligns pixel-for-pixel with it. Do not reframe, regenerate or regularize the scene. Object boxes above use native coordinates: multiply by FOUR for input/output pixels. Preserve actual object dimensions under the fixed camera and perspective. Do not shrink targets to fit destinations or shrink whole stacks. Move targets with their original shape/volume. Preserve the named arms mechanical identity and its connection to its original fixed mount. An arm may reach across the table; target position and the edge where cropped gripper appears do not define arm identity. Do not mirror the robot or exchange arms. [final-extent guides] Image 3 also includes ORANGE final-extent guides: manually proposed geometric layout derived from initial object dimensions and the instruction, NOT an observed future image. Match the original objects size and shape within this guide at its destination. These outlines are approximate projections, never additional objects. Remove all guide lines/text from the output. Do not treat an orange guide as an initial object or duplicate the target. [relocation guides] IMPORTANT IMAGE-3 SIZE / POSE GUIDE: the orange-outlined target at the destination is an exact unscaled cutout of the initial object, translated to propose the final placement. It is synthetic guidance from initial pixels, NOT future observation or an additional object. This guide makes the required size and yaw explicit: match that FULL-SIZE silhouette and pose, keep the destination mat fixed underneath, and remove the old source object. Generate coherent final scene with natural contact/shadows, without orange outlines or text. Do not shrink the target to fit inside the mat. FINAL IMAGE CHECKS -- every item must be visibly satisfied: {acceptance_checks} (expands to one bullet per check) [edit masks] The attached alpha mask restricts editing to transparent regions containing the old target and proposed destination. Keep opaque regions exactly unchanged. Render the completed object placement inside the editable regions; do not move fixed supports or resize targets to fit the mask. No robot arm needs to enter completed released-placement scene. PUBLIC OFFICIAL COMPLETE TASK -- authoritative over the historical reference example: Task: {task} Full description: {robotwin_full_description} Official placeholder schema: {robotwin_schema} Preserve the exact current official instruction, including explicit release, put-down and negation clauses. Only after recorded compatibility review may the complete task fill in omitted steps. An explicit contradictory instruction is not an omission and must not be silently overridden. Unresolved language conflicts require review before generation. Left/right arm names refer to the robots mechanical arms and their fixed mounts, not the targets horizontal image position or the edge where cropped gripper appears. Preserve each arms connection to its own mount, including cross-table reaches; do not mirror the robot or exchange arm identities. The appearance sheet illustrates construction only. Official {A}/{B} placeholders and historical annotation object IDs A/B are separate namespaces: rebuild their role mapping from current initial RGB and instruction, never equate letters. Preserve current object identity, size and background. The public complete task takes precedence over any reference plan, fixed flag, mask or acceptance check that would prevent required motion, lifting, holding, transfer or placement. Do not keep support stationary when this task requires lifting or moving that support. Do not depict an intermediate placement as the completed task. Use no expert future RGB, trajectory, future pose, simulator state or hidden instance information. REVIEWED QUALITATIVE GOAL QUALITY GUIDANCE: This is reviewed image guidance derived from existing public task semantics; it is not new official requirement or an assertion that generated image proves physical success. It must remain compatible with the exact current instruction. Success may occur earlier in trajectory; do not replace explicit current-language actions with guessed terminal rule. {task_guidance} (expands to one bullet per guidance line) Example. For blocks_ranking_size with the instruction Align large block, medium block, and small block by size from left to right at the center., the scene-specific parts of the editing prompt are: GROUNDED INITIAL OBJECTS (pixel boxes use Image 1s 288x224 coordinates): - L: large purple block; initial box [52, 78, 90, 116]. - M: medium light green block; initial box [230, 92, 265, 131]. - S: small magenta block; initial box [106, 105, 126, 130]. REQUIRED FINAL STATE: Move the three blocks to central tabletop row and align them by physical size from left to right: L, the large purple block, on the left; M, the medium light green block, in the middle; S, the small magenta block, on the right. Keep the blocks upright, preserve their current colors and dimensions, leave small gaps between them, do not stack them, and release all blocks after placement. The completed row should be centered on the table around the middle of the image rather than leaving far to the right or between and M. FINAL IMAGE CHECKS -- every item must be visibly satisfied: - Exactly the three visible blocks are arranged at the table center in one horizontal row. - Left-to-right order is largest to smallest: large purple L, medium light green M, then small magenta S. - All blocks remain upright, unstacked, non-overlapping, and released on the tabletop. - No unrelated scene elements are moved or newly introduced. Full description: there are three blocks on the table, the color of the blocks is random, move the blocks to the center of the table, and arrange them from largest to smallest, from left to right REVIEWED QUALITATIVE GOAL QUALITY GUIDANCE: - Identify large, medium and small using their true current physical dimensions, not color. Place the same three blocks in central tabletop row with largest left, medium middle and smallest right, preserving all dimensions and colors. - Small-then-medium-then-large wording specifies handling order; it does not reverse the final left-to-right size order given by full_description. Follow named per-block arms and depict completed released placement rather than stacking or holding block. 51 Table 15 First-pass review outcomes for the 7,032 newly generated evaluation goal images. Verdict Images Share Pass Fail Uncertain 6,380 542 110 90.7% 7.7% 1.6% Total 7,032 100.0% A.4 Goal Review and Repair ChatGPT Astra High reviews every newly generated evaluation goal image. For each case it sees the initial and generated head images at native resolution, the instruction, the public task description, and the Stage-1 grounding. It treats the grounding as fallible and locates objects independently in the initial image, then returns pass, fail, or uncertain with case-specific evidence. The review rubric is: Check target/destination identity, exact instructed goal relation/arm when visually distinguishable, source removal/object counts, appearance/size, fixed background/destination/camera, real grasp/contact/support, articulated hinge, and coherent robot. Public full task only fills omissions compatibly, never overrides explicit instruction. Natural occlusion is legitimate. Do not demand an entire trajectory in single goal frame, invent new acceptance rules, equate image-side with mechanical arm, or mark all cropped mounts uncertain. Pass means visible state is consistent with no clear defect; fail means concrete visible contradiction; uncertain identifies concrete unresolved evidence. The audit concerns whether the visible generated goal is compatible with the exact task under the fixed head camera; it does NOT establish hidden physical state or execution history. If the requested endpoint is naturally outside the view or inside clipped container, all relevant visible changes and fixed geometry are consistent, and no visible contradiction exists, use pass with an explicit visibility limitation. Retain uncertain when there is specific visible ambiguity (which physical object, actual contact, orientation, scale) rather than merely unverifiable hidden physics. Repair. Each non-passing verdict (fail or uncertain) comes with repair feedback and repair stage. If the grounding misidentified the source, receiver, or contact region, the reviewer supplies corrected target from the initial image and Stage 1 is rerun with this feedback. Otherwise, Stage 2 is rerun with the feedback inserted before the task block, and the grounding is kept. Every replacement image is reviewed again. Regenerated images are judged under looser criterion than first-pass images: the reviewer accepts reasonable perspective variation and mild size differences that can be explained by projection, but still rejects wrong targets or receivers, duplicated or missing objects, wrong task relations, severe deformation, invented fixtures, and disconnected or extra arms.
